linkedin.commentary:
Is it a secondary injury, or is it a side effect?

Most claim files can't answer that question.

A worker injures their back. Three months later the file shows dizziness, low mood, poor sleep, a fall at home.

Each one gets assessed as a new condition.
Each one gets treated.
Each one can become a liability the insurer or employer ends up funding.

Sometimes it is a consequential injury. Often it is the medication.

Opioids can cause low mood and poor sleep.
Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs can cause unsteadiness and memory problems.
Gabapentinoids can cause dizziness and drowsiness.
Antidepressants and antipsychotics can cause weight gain and sedation.

In a claim, those effects rarely get labelled as adverse effects. They get labelled as something else.

AllMeds reads the medication history first, flags the adverse effect risk, and shows claims teams what to act on before a side effect becomes a diagnosis.

Find it early, or fund it later.

posts.title: How a side effect becomes an accepted condition

linkedin.commentary:
How a side effect becomes an accepted condition:

1. A medication is prescribed for the injury.
2. It causes an adverse effect.
3. The adverse effect is read as a new condition.
4. A new medication is prescribed to treat it.
5. Repeat.

By step five, the claim has a secondary condition, a longer medication list and a return to work date that keeps moving.

Nobody did anything wrong. Nobody was looking at the medications as a whole.

That is the gap AllMeds closes. It assesses the full medication list, identifies where an adverse effect is the more likely explanation, and gives the case manager a clear next step while the problem is still small.

The cheapest secondary injury is the one that never gets diagnosed, because it was never an injury.

posts.title: A medication review shouldn't have to wait for a referral

linkedin.commentary:
A medication review shouldn't have to wait for a referral.

Medicine-related problems put an estimated 250,000 Australians in hospital every year. Another 400,000 end up in emergency. At least half of that harm is considered preventable.

Australia has a program built to prevent it. The Home Medicines Review (HMR) has run since 2001.

But a review only happens if a GP or listed specialist refers. The person who needs it can't ask for one. Neither can their family or their pharmacist.

In 2025-26, about 180,915 people had an HMR. 1.9 million Australians take five or more medicines.

That is fewer than one review for every ten people who need one.

This week we are setting out why the HMR model no longer fits the Australian public, and what we are proposing instead.

Medication reviews for every Australian, not only the referred.

Sources: Pharmaceutical Society of Australia, Medicine Safety: Take Care (2019). HMR Program Rules (2026). Australian Pharmacist (2026). AIHW, Polypharmacy in Australia in 2025.

#MedicineSafety #HomeMedicinesReview #HealthPolicy

posts.title: Medication reviews keep people out of hospital. When they happen

linkedin.commentary:
Medication reviews keep people out of hospital. When they happen.

The evidence is not in question.

Australian veterans with heart failure who had an HMR had a 45% lower rate of heart failure admissions.

Veterans on warfarin were 79% less likely to be admitted for bleeding in the 2 to 6 months after an HMR.

Across 20 trials, pharmacist-led medication reviews cut hospital admissions by 19%.

Two things make it work: the review happens, and a doctor acts on it.

The HMR keeps the doctor. It rations the review.

Only by referral. One per person every 24 months. 30 per pharmacist a month.

The warfarin benefit faded after six months, and the researchers suggested six-monthly reviews for high-risk patients. The program allows one every two years.

Last year there was fewer than one HMR for every ten Australians on five or more medicines. The barrier isn't the review. It's access.

Sources: Roughead EE et al, Circ Heart Fail 2009 and J Clin Pharm Ther 2011. Khalil H et al, Drug Saf 2025. HMR Program Rules (2026). Australian Pharmacist (2026). AIHW (2025).

#MedicineSafety #HomeMedicinesReview #HealthPolicy

posts.title: In rural Australia, a medication review starts with a long drive

linkedin.commentary:
In rural Australia, a medication review starts with a long drive.

The first HMR interview must happen face to face, in the patient's home. That means a pharmacist driving out to every patient.

Travel time isn't paid. The rural loading is a flat $125 at most, and only for round trips of 200 km or more. Pharmacists report driving an hour to a patient and still not qualifying.

The $222.77 fee hasn't been indexed since July 2019. One western Queensland pharmacist has described the program as non-viable once travel and accommodation are counted.

So the people furthest from a pharmacist wait the longest. The profession itself reports that rural, remote and First Nations Australians are the most affected.

Meanwhile, rural and remote Australia carries an estimated 72,500 medication-related hospital admissions a year, at a cost of $400 million.

A review that depends on a long drive won't reach the people who need it most. The fix isn't more driving. It's removing the drive.

Sources: PSA, Medicine Safety: Rural and Remote Care. HMR Program Rules (2026). Australian Pharmacist (2026). PSA, Uncap care and media release (2026).

#RuralHealth #HomeMedicinesReview #MedicineSafety

posts.title: Three doctors. Seven medicines. Nobody sees all seven

linkedin.commentary:
Three doctors. Seven medicines. Nobody sees all seven.

Picture an older Australian in a regional town. Their GP prescribes four medicines for blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes and reflux. A telehealth doctor adds a sleep medicine after one video consult. A specialist interstate adds a pain medicine and a nerve pain medicine. Three pharmacies dispense them.

Seven medicines. Three of them sedating. No single doctor or pharmacy sees the whole list. (Illustrative example. Not a real patient.)

This is increasingly common. 399 million electronic prescriptions have been issued since May 2020. 17.8% of Australians saw three or more health professionals for the same condition in 2024-25, up from 15.1% in 2018-19. Of those, 28.8% had nobody coordinating their care.

Under the HMR model, a review depends on one of those doctors, each seeing part of the list, deciding to refer.

A patient-led review flips it. The patient lists all seven. With their consent, every prescribing doctor gets the same findings.

Nobody sees 7 becomes every doctor sees 7.

Sources: Australian Digital Health Agency (to August 2025). ABS, Patient Experiences 2024-25 and 2018-19.

#MedicineSafety #DigitalHealth #HomeMedicinesReview

posts.title: What if the patient could start their own medication review?

linkedin.commentary:
What if the patient could start their own medication review?

That is the model we are proposing for the Home Medicines Review program.

1. The patient starts, from home, on a phone or computer, with a carer or family member if they wish. No referral needed.

2. Every medicine is checked, from every prescriber and every pharmacy, for interactions, adverse effects, duplication and high-risk prescribing. Risk rated in minutes.

3. With the patient's consent, the findings go to their prescribing doctors, led by the GP or doctor they nominate.

4. The doctors decide what changes. Clinical responsibility stays with them.

No pharmacist drives to the home. Two AllMeds pharmacists oversee every risk assessment, remotely.

No extra appointments either. The patient's doctors already see them regularly, so the findings are acted on at the next Medicare-funded visit. Only critical cases need an extra appointment, and those would be justified anyway.

A doctor can still refer for an HMR where an in-home assessment is needed.

$150 flat, wherever the patient lives. No travel. No loading.

AllMeds is an Australian AI medication risk platform governed by pharmacists. It provides medication information and risk insights. It does not prescribe, and it does not replace the doctor.

#HomeMedicinesReview #RuralHealth #DigitalHealth

posts.title: A 1,000-patient rural pilot. Then the evidence decides

linkedin.commentary:
A 1,000-patient rural pilot. Then the evidence decides.

About 378,000 Australians aged 65 and over who take five or more medicines live in rural and regional Australia.

Reviewing each of them every 24 months:

Through the HMR with rural loading: $65.7 million a year, and about 525 pharmacists working at the cap, all driving.

Through AllMeds: $28.4 million a year, overseen by two pharmacists, remotely.

A rural medication-related admission costs about $5,500. At $28.4 million, the patient-led model pays for itself if it prevents about 1 in 14 rural medication-related admissions. That is a break-even threshold, not a forecast. It is what a pilot should test.

So that is what we are asking for: a funded pilot for 1,000 Australians aged 65 and over in rural and regional Australia, paid from within the Home Medicines Review program, independently evaluated before any national rollout.

The measure of success: more Australians reviewed, sooner, with nobody travelling, and fewer medication-related hospital admissions.

Medication reviews for every Australian, not only the referred.

Figures: AllMeds modelling on Quek HW et al (2025), AIHW, PSA Medicine Safety reports and the HMR Program Rules (2026).

#HomeMedicinesReview #RuralHealth #HealthPolicy
